corpus_definition: to continue doing something even when it is difficult

forms.definition: the quality of not stopping when something is hard
forms.example: Her persistence helped her pass the exam on the third try.

syn.note: Very close: a strong wish to do something even when it is hard.
Almost the same meaning; a little more formal.
Related: being calm while you wait or keep trying.

forms.definition: to keep doing something even when it is hard
forms.example: He persisted with his English lessons although he was very busy.

syn.note: Continue is general; persist means you go on even when it is difficult.
Easy, everyday phrasal verb with a similar meaning.
Informal and easy: do not stop.
Very close; a little more formal.

ant.note: To stop trying because something is too hard.
To stop doing something, often before it is finished.

forms.definition: not stopping trying, even when others say no
forms.example: The persistent salesman called us every day for a week.
forms.note: Also means 'lasting a long time': a persistent cough, persistent rain.

syn.note: Close: you really want to do it and will not stop.
Related but negative: not willing to change your mind.

forms.definition: in a way that continues and does not stop
forms.example: The child persistently asked for ice cream.

syn.note: Related: all the time, again and again.
Related: many times; persistently adds the idea of not giving up.

context.text: Aziz failed his driving test twice, but he persisted. His teacher said his persistence was the reason he finally passed.

reviewer_note: persistent also has a 'lasting' sense (persistent cough); kept in a note on the adjective.

corpus_definition: To make someone agree with you by talking.

forms.definition: the act of making someone agree or do something by talking
forms.example: After a lot of persuasion, my father let me go to the concert.

syn.note: The act of making someone believe or agree.
Related: the power to change what people think or do.

forms.definition: to make someone agree or do something by giving reasons
forms.example: I persuaded my sister to come to Samarkand with us.

syn.note: Very close. convince someone to do something = persuade someone to do something.
Informal phrasal verb: 'She talked me into buying it.'
Related: you give support, but the person may still say no.
Related: you ask strongly; it does not mean they agree.

ant.note: Formal: to make someone decide NOT to do something.
To try to stop someone from doing something.

forms.definition: good at making people agree with you
forms.example: She gave a very persuasive speech about saving water.

syn.note: Very close: it makes you believe it is true.
Strong and interesting, so you have to agree.

ant.note: Not able to make people believe or agree.

forms.definition: in a way that makes people agree with you
forms.example: He spoke so persuasively that everyone voted for his plan.

syn.note: Very close in meaning.

context.text: My friend tried to persuade me to join the football team. He was very persuasive, so I said yes.

reviewer_note: persuasion/persuasive change the stem (persuade -> persuas-), so no -sion/-ive affix is claimed; dissuade is a separate word, used only as an antonym.

corpus_definition: The state of your body being strong and free from sickness.
usage_note: Uncountable noun phrase: good / poor physical health; for your physical health; often paired with mental health: 'physical and mental health'.

relations.note: Related: how strong your body is, mostly from exercise.
More general: it can mean the body, the mind, or both.
Wider: feeling healthy and happy in body and mind. US spelling: well-being.
Not the same: it is about your mind, not your body. The two are often used together.
The state of being sick in your body.

context.text: Walking every day is good for your physical health. My grandmother is 80, but her physical health is still very good.

reviewer_note: Fixed noun phrase; mental health listed as related, not as an antonym.

corpus_definition: A tall evergreen tree with thin sharp leaves.

forms.definition: a tall tree with thin, sharp leaves that stay green all year
forms.example: We had a picnic under the pine trees in the mountains near Chimgan.
forms.note: Also the wood of this tree: a pine table.

syn.note: Related: any tree with cones and thin leaves; pine is one kind.
Related: another tall evergreen tree that looks similar.
Related: any tree that keeps its leaves all year.

forms.note: The verb pine (to feel very sad because you miss someone: pine for home) is a different word with the same spelling, not part of the tree family.
Use the noun before another noun: pine forest, pine wood.

context.text: There is a beautiful pine forest in the mountains. In winter the pine trees are still green.

reviewer_note: Homonym trap: verb pine (to miss) is etymologically a separate word, so it is not shown as a family form. Compounds (pine cone, pineapple) left out.

corpus_definition: A large deep hole in the ground.

forms.definition: a large deep hole in the ground
forms.example: The workers dug a pit to plant the old tree.
forms.note: Also a coal mine (UK), and in American English the hard seed of some fruit.

syn.note: Easy, general word; a pit is usually large and deep.
Related: a low place in the ground, not always deep.
Related: a large round hole made by something hitting the ground.
Related: a long narrow hole next to a road or field.

ant.note: A small hill or pile of earth that rises above the ground.

forms.definition: to make a person or team compete against another
forms.example: The final will pit the two best teams against each other.
forms.note: Belongs to pit = a place where animals were made to fight; used as 'pit A against B', not about digging holes.

forms.definition: covered with small holes or marks
forms.example: The old road was pitted with small holes after the winter.
forms.note: Belongs to pit = a small mark or hole on a surface, not a large hole in the ground.

context.text: Near the village there is an old pit where people once took sand for building. Now it is full of rainwater in spring.

reviewer_note: Verb 'pit against' and adjective 'pitted' kept as other_meaning; compounds (armpit, pitfall) left out.

corpus_definition: A feeling of sadness for someone else's trouble.

forms.definition: a feeling of sadness for a person or animal in trouble
forms.example: I felt pity for the lost dog in the rain.
forms.note: 'It's a pity' means 'it's sad or disappointing': It's a pity you can't come.

syn.note: Close: you understand and share someone's sadness.
Close and stronger: you feel sorry and want to help.
Related: deep sadness, often about your own loss.

ant.note: Not caring at all about someone's trouble.

forms.definition: to feel sorry for someone because they are in trouble
forms.example: I pity anyone who has to drive in this snow.

syn.note: Easy, everyday phrase with the same meaning.
Understand and share someone's feelings. British spelling: sympathise.

forms.definition: making you feel sad and sorry for someone
forms.example: The hungry kitten made a pitiful sound.
forms.note: Informally it can also mean 'very bad': a pitiful excuse.

syn.note: Close; in informal English it often means 'very bad' too.
Easy, general word for unhappy things.
Related: very unhappy or in a very bad state.

forms.definition: cruel and feeling no sadness for others
forms.example: The pitiless sun burned the fields all summer.

syn.note: Easy word: wanting others to suffer or not caring.
Very close: having no kind feelings.

ant.note: Kind and ready to forgive or help.
Feeling sorry for others and wanting to help.

forms.definition: showing that you feel sorry for someone
forms.example: She gave me a pitying look when I dropped my phone.

forms.definition: in a way that makes people feel sad and sorry
forms.example: The little boy cried pitifully when he lost his mother in the market.

syn.note: Close; can also mean 'very badly'.
Easy, general word.

context.text: We found a cat with a hurt leg near the bazaar. It looked so pitiful that we all felt pity for it and took it to a vet.

reviewer_note: 'It's a pity' (= shame) noted on the noun; pitiable/piteous are rare and left out.

corpus_definition: A large area of land where crops are grown.

forms.definition: a large farm where one crop, like cotton or tea, is grown
forms.example: They work on a large coffee plantation in Brazil.

syn.note: Close: a large area of land, often a tea or coffee estate.
Easy, general word; a plantation is usually very big and grows one crop.
Related: land with fruit trees, usually smaller.

forms.definition: a living thing with roots and leaves that grows in soil
forms.example: My mother has many plants in the garden.
forms.note: Also a factory or power station: a power plant.

syn.note: Related: plants that farmers grow for food or money.

forms.definition: to put seeds or young trees in the ground to grow
forms.example: Farmers plant cotton in April in Uzbekistan.

syn.note: Close, but only for seeds: sow wheat.
Related: to take care of plants so they get bigger.

ant.note: To pull a plant out of the ground with its roots.
To collect the crop at the end of the season.

people.definition: a person who owns or manages a large farm growing one crop
people.example: The tea planter showed us his fields.
people.note: Also a large pot for growing plants.

context.text: My uncle works on a big tea plantation. Every spring the workers plant new bushes, and every summer they pick the leaves.

reviewer_note: plantation is made from plant (noun/verb); plant noun shown as an extra in the noun slot. Historical slavery sense of plantation not mentioned.

corpus_definition: Full of energy and wanting to have fun.

forms.definition: the quality of being full of fun and energy
forms.example: We love the playfulness of our new puppy.

syn.note: Easy word: enjoyment and pleasure.
Related: being full of energy.

forms.definition: activities that children do for fun
forms.example: Children learn a lot through play.

forms.definition: to do things for fun, like games or sport
forms.example: The children played in the park all afternoon.

syn.note: Easy phrase: enjoy yourself.
Do something to pass the time in a fun way.

ant.note: To do a job or a task, not for fun.

forms.definition: full of energy and wanting to have fun
forms.example: The puppy was very playful this morning.
forms.note: Also 'not serious, joking': a playful smile.

syn.note: Close: someone who enjoys having fun.
Related: full of energy.
Related: happy and positive.
Related: playful in a slightly naughty way.

forms.definition: in a fun way that is not serious
forms.example: She playfully threw a snowball at her brother.

syn.note: Close: as a joke.
Related: joking with someone in a friendly way.

ant.note: In a way that is not joking.

people.definition: a person who takes part in a game or sport
people.example: Each player gets five cards at the start.

context.text: Our cat is very playful in the morning. She likes to play with a ball and playfully jumps on my feet.

reviewer_note: Headword is the adjective; verb and noun play are the base of the family. Compounds (playground, playmate) left out.

corpus_definition: The series of events that form the story of a book.

forms.definition: the events that make up the story of a book or film
forms.example: The movie has a very complex plot.
forms.note: Other meanings: a secret plan to do something bad; a small piece of land (a garden plot).

syn.note: Almost the same meaning.
Easy word; story can mean the whole book, plot is the order of events.
More formal word for a story.

forms.definition: to plan the events of a story
forms.example: The writer plotted the whole novel before she wrote the first page.
forms.note: More often it means 'to plan something bad in secret': They plotted to steal the money.

syn.note: Related: to decide what will happen.
Related: to give the main points of a story.

people.definition: a person who makes secret plans to do something bad
people.example: The police caught the plotters before they could act.
people.note: Belongs to plot = a secret plan, not the story of a book.

context.text: I didn't like the plot of the new film. It felt like the writers plotted it in one afternoon.

reviewer_note: Senses: story (kept), secret plan and piece of land (noted); plotter is other_meaning.

corpus_definition: To draw attention to a specific fact.
particle_note: Separable: 'point out the mistake' or 'point the mistake out'; with a pronoun only 'point it out'. Often followed by a that-clause: 'She pointed out that the shop was closed.' Also 'point something out to someone'.

relations.note: Same meaning; a little more formal.
Formal: show or say something clearly.
Related: say something quickly, without making it important.
To not notice or not mention something.
To pay no attention to something on purpose.

context.text: My teacher pointed out two mistakes in my essay. She also pointed out that my ideas were very good.

reviewer_note: Literal 'point out = show with your finger' is not the corpus sense; kept to drawing attention to a fact.
